title: From the Unknown to the Desired: Transforming Unknown Initial States in the Resource Theory of Work and Heat
abstract: We study thermodynamic state transformations in the resource theory of work and heat when the initial quantum state is unknown. Moving beyond state-dependent protocols, we develop a universal framework in which a single transformation applies to all admissible input states. For mutually commuting conserved charges, we construct charge-conserving protocols whose transformation error, quantified by trace distance, decays super-polynomially with the number of system copies. As an application, we demonstrate universal work extraction: asymptotically optimal work can be extracted without microscopic knowledge of the initial state, with a super-polynomially small error. Our results show that thermodynamic state transformations remain achievable under limited prior information and establish a universal framework for resource-theoretic thermodynamics beyond the state-aware setting.
summary: This theoretical work develops a universal framework for quantum thermodynamics applicable when the initial quantum state is unknown. By analyzing the state within a 'charge-entropy equivalence class,' the authors show that optimal work extraction remains achievable asymptotically. The key breakthrough is developing measurement protocols that estimate necessary state parameters with minimal disturbance, thus extending resource theory beyond state-aware settings.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to perform thermodynamic state transformations (work and heat) when the initial quantum state is unknown, moving beyond protocols that require full state knowledge.
main_result: A universal, reference-frame-free framework is established showing that optimal work extraction can be achieved asymptotically even without microscopic knowledge of the initial state.
method: The authors develop protocols based on the charge-entropy equivalence class, utilizing coarse-grained measurements on multiple copies of the state to estimate necessary thermodynamic parameters.
model_or_system: The study concerns quantum thermodynamic state transformations for i.i.d. copies of a quantum state $ho$ in a general Hilbert space, analyzed within the resource theory of work and heat.
key_observables: Entropy $S(ho)$, expectation values of mutually commuting conserved charges $	ext{Tr}(ho L_i)$, and the transformation error (quantified by trace distance).
important_parameters: The number of system copies ($n$), the decay rate of the transformation error (super-polynomial decay), and the required accuracy of state estimation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the existence of a charge-entropy equivalence class and relies on the ability to estimate entropy and charges with vanishingly small disturbance using coarse-grained measurements.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the conversion of an $n$-copy state into its charge–entropy normal form; Figure 2 illustrates the transformation between two states in the same class using an ancilla, showing the error decay.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the universal framework for state transformations within an equivalence class, then developing techniques to estimate the necessary state parameters (entropy and charges) from unknown copies, and finally applying this to demonstrate universal work extraction.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful generalization of resource theories, showing that fundamental thermodynamic limits can be robustly established even when experimental measurements are inherently limited by incomplete state knowledge.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Conversion of an n-copy i.i.d. state ρ⊗n into its charge– entropy normal form by a unitary V that depends only on the charge– entropy equivalence class containing ρ. The first component is max- imally mixed, with its dimension and associated charges determined solely by the entropy and average charges of ρ, whereas the second component retains the explicit dependence on ρ, with its associated charge operators depending explicitly on the total charges L×n c .

FIG. 2. Transformation of ρ⊗n into σ⊗n, where ρ and σ belong to the same charge–entropy equivalence class, assisted by a sublinear- sized ancilla. The unitary V maps ρ⊗n to the charge–entropy normal form τ(E) ⊗η(K) ρ with error at most δ(ϵn). Since the linearly supported component τ(E) is identical for states within the same charge–entropy equivalence class, the desired transformation is achieved by swap- ping η(K) ρ with an ancilla prepared in the state η(K) σ , followed by V†. The total transformation error is at most 2δ(ϵn), accounting for the errors incurred in applying V and V†.

FIG. 3. Schematic illustration of universal thermodynamic state transformations from unknown quantum states. Given n copies of an unknown initial state ρ⊗n, one first performs a charge-preserving measurement to estimate the entropy and average charges. Once these quantities are determined, one applies a state-transformation protocol that depends only on the estimated entropy and average charges. Combining these two steps—estimation of the entropy and average charges, followed by the corresponding state-transformation protocol—yields a universal transformation protocol.

FIG. 4. Energy–entropy diagram illustrating the maximum ex- tractable work per copy from ρ. The diagram shows that, to extract the maximum amount of work from ρ, one must transform it into the Gibbs state τρ that has the same entropy as ρ and is defined with re- spect to the same Hamiltonian.
